newsitem.title: UK: Analysts give Sainsbury's Bank cautious welcome.
newsitem.headline: Analysts give Sainsbury's Bank cautious welcome.

text.p: Banking analysts on Friday gave a cautious welcome to the announcement that British supermarket retailer Sainsbury is to set up a banking division with the Bank of Scotland.
"The point is they (Sainsbury) can't do it alone...and they can't necessarily go out and take bank business away," one banking analyst told Reuters.

The new bank -- to be called Sainsbury's Bank -- will be 55 percent owned by Sainsbury, with Bank of Scotland taking the remaining stake. The move goes one step beyond other ventures into financial services by supermarket groups.

The first analyst said the venture would not harm the Bank of Scotland's position, adding that it could help the bank to gain a greater foothold away from its traditional stronghold in Scotland. But the push south of the border into England would involve relatively low costs, he added.
"It's not going to do them (Bank of Scotland) any harm at all. It will give them very low cost distribution," he said.

This view was backed by Peter Toeman, analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett who said Bank of Scotland had always been "hamstrung by a lack of branches outside Scotland" but had developed "innovative non-traditional distribution channels".
As a result Bank of Scotland, with experience and capacity for credit cards and consumer loans, was well positioned to offer these services to the new bank, Toeman added.
Both credit cards and consumer finance continued to offer "very, very attractive returns" due to the high rates and the attractive spreads banks were able to maintain.
This meant both were "areas of focus for all the banks" because they could provide the highest returns on capital, of around 40 percent after tax, Toeman said.
"The banks have always felt that the threat was not going to come from existing players," he added.

"You don't need a branch network, so the barriers to entry have fallen," he said. This meant players such as British Telecom, Sainsbury and Tesco were likely to become the major competitors of the future.

While Sainsbury's Bank was unlikely to get into unprofitable cheque-book accounts, it could provide a basic branch network in the form of kiosks in its branches in the same way as Marks & Spencer has done to market financial services.
Toeman said the new bank should have no problem in being granted a banking licence, but said the capitalisation would depend on the amount it lent out.

The first analyst said the new bank "would do limited damage" to the existing high street banks, adding that most Sainsbury customers were likely to have bank accounts already and the terms offered would not necessarily be better.
For Bank of Scotland there could be "a marginal enhancement in their earnings profile", but the analyst said he would not be raising his profit forecast for the bank.

Toeman agreed that the venture would not take a large market share, but said it would make it hard for the banks to extend their credit card operations and could have an impact on the pricing strategy.
